rationale: Start with a broad gradient to survey retention and separation of all 10 compounds while allowing a substantial high-organic hold for late eluters. A midrange temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

Halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty while testing how much of the current resolution margin can be retained. Keep temperature and endpoints fixed to isolate the effect of gradient steepness.

Keep the fast gradient and raise temperature to test whether temperature-dependent selectivity separates the crowded middle peaks. This targets the resolution penalty while aiming to retain the zero time penalty.

Test a smaller temperature increase to improve the remaining close pair while monitoring the narrowing gap elsewhere in the middle cluster. Keep the gradient fixed to map temperature selectivity without sacrificing the zero time penalty.

Slightly flatten the gradient to improve the newly limiting middle pair at 55 C. The last peak should still elute early enough to avoid a time penalty, while this run tests whether both critical gaps can exceed 1.5.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; test a slightly shallower gradient to explore nearby methods with the same score. This may strengthen the 1.59-resolution gap while keeping the last peak close to the zero-time-penalty window; the 1.52 gap needs monitoring.

With the maximum score already secured, test a higher starting organic fraction for a potentially faster method with comparable separation. Monitor both close middle pairs and early-peak retention, since changing the starting composition can alter selectivity.

Slightly flatten the gradient from injection 7 to improve its limiting 1.29-resolution pair while retaining the stronger separation of the other critical pair. This may provide another maximum-score method with the last peak still below 8 minutes.

Extend the trend from injections 7–8 with a slightly shallower gradient, aiming to bring both critical resolutions above 1.5. The projected last-peak time is approximately 8 minutes, near the observed zero-penalty boundary.

With the maximum CRF already secured, explore a substantially faster gradient at higher temperature for an alternative selectivity regime. This tests whether the crowded middle peaks separate after an elution-order reversal, though resolution may deteriorate.

The maximum score is already secured, so explore low-temperature selectivity as an alternative route to full separation with a fast gradient. Cooling may open the crowded middle cluster, but could create a different limiting pair.

Return to the successful 55 C selectivity and combine a higher starting organic fraction with a longer gradient. This tests whether reduced retention can offset the longer gradient while preserving full resolution and a zero time penalty.

Match injection 5’s successful gradient slope of 0.075 organic fraction per minute, but end the gradient earlier at a lower organic fraction. Since all peaks previously eluted before this new gradient endpoint reaches the outlet, the separation and maximum CRF should be preserved.

Test a gradient slope between injections 8 and 9 to balance their two critical separations. This should keep the last peak below 8 minutes while potentially retaining full resolution with slightly more margin than injection 5.

Preserve injection 5’s successful gradient slope while lowering the endpoint and shortening the programmed gradient. The endpoint reaches the outlet at 8.65 minutes, after the observed last peak at 7.60 minutes, so the maximum-score separation should be retained.

Keep the successful gradient slope through the closely spaced peaks, then test a lower-organic hold for elution of the isolated final peak. This explores whether the maximum CRF can be retained with a shorter programmed gradient, although delayed final elution could introduce a time penalty.

Slightly flatten the gradient relative to injection 9 to improve its 1.67-resolution pair while checking that the other critical pair remains above 1.5. The last peak is expected near 8.2 minutes, within the zero-time-penalty range demonstrated by injection 16.

Flatten the gradient relative to injection 12 to improve its limiting middle pair while exploiting the stronger separation of the other critical pair. This tests for a maximum-score method with greater resolution margin, although later final elution may introduce a time penalty.

Preserve injection 9’s successful slope and starting composition while reducing the endpoint and programmed gradient duration. Since the endpoint reaches the outlet at 8.65 minutes, after the previous final peak at 8.00 minutes, the maximum CRF should be retained.

With the maximum CRF already secured, test the upper-temperature neighbor of injection 5 to assess temperature sensitivity. This isolates the temperature effect at the successful gradient and checks whether a faster, fully resolved alternative exists.

Test the lower-temperature neighbor of the optimal method to complete the local temperature-sensitivity check. The maximum score is already secured; this run will determine whether cooling preserves full resolution or compresses the other critical middle pair.

Return to 55 C and slightly flatten injection 17’s gradient to map the maximum-score region. The limiting resolution should remain near 1.5, while the projected final elution around 8.6 minutes is within the demonstrated zero-penalty range.

Test a lower endpoint with a slope close to injection 22’s maximum-score method. The critical middle peaks should remain resolved; the final peak will probe whether the lower-organic hold preserves the zero time penalty.

Test a slightly steeper gradient than injection 14 to locate the faster edge of the maximum-score region. This should shorten final elution, though the middle pair with resolution 1.55 may fall below 1.5.

For the final injection, test a slope between the maximum-score methods from injections 17 and 22, where both critical pairs should remain resolved without a time penalty. The campaign has already reached the theoretical maximum CRF of 1.000.
